analysis.one_liner: Replaces consumer bankruptcy with a single streamlined chapter that lets struggling households erase more debt, including mortgages and student loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 8, 2020 with one cosponsor, referred to two committees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite consumer bankruptcy from scratch. It replaces the current two-track system, where people either liquidate their assets under Chapter 7 or commit to a multi-year repayment plan under Chapter 13, with one new process, Chapter 10, for people with under $7.5 million in debt. People with little or no ability to pay could get their debts wiped out quickly with almost no paperwork, and everyone else would pay only what a formula based on their income and assets says they can afford. It would also let bankruptcy judges change the terms of home mortgages and car loans, make most student loan debt erasable like other debt, and create a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
analysis.who_benefits: Households crushed by debt they cannot pay, especially people who today cannot afford a lawyer or cannot finish a Chapter 13 repayment plan. The bill's own findings say people lose work to job loss, medical bills, and educational debt, that the current system produces racially disparate outcomes, and that many debtors must save up just to pay an attorney to file.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a single Chapter 10 bankruptcy for individual debtors, eliminating Chapter 7 liquidation for individuals and repealing Chapter 13 repayment plans [S2].

Allows debtors with a minimum payment obligation of zero to receive a discharge without filing any plan, and others to discharge debts by paying what a formula based on their income and assets requires [S3].
Permits modification of mortgages on all residences and of car loans to the market value of the vehicle, and allows student loan debt to be discharged on equal terms with most other debt [S2].

Lets debtors run limited, lighter-weight bankruptcy proceedings aimed at specific debts such as a home mortgage, and creates a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau [S2].
States goals of lowering the cost of filing, reducing racial and gender disparities in bankruptcy outcomes, and closing loopholes that let wealthy debtors shield assets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other consumer lenders, mortgage holders, private student loan companies, auto lenders, and debt collectors, whose claims would be dischargeable or reduced more often than under current law. These costs could be passed back to all borrowers through tighter credit terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, mortgage and student loan lenders

drawbacks.text: Creditors would recover less from bankruptcy cases, and lenders would likely respond by tightening credit terms or raising rates for all borrowers, including people who never file [S3].

Repealing Chapter 13 and Chapter 7 for individuals and standing up an entirely new chapter would be one of the largest rewrites of the Bankruptcy Code since 1978, a transition courts, trustees, and lenders would need years to absorb [S3].
Allowing modification of mortgages on all residences reverses a rule lenders have operated under since 2005; the mortgage industry would argue this raises the cost and risk of mortgage lending [S2].

Discharge once every six years and immediate discharge for zero-payment debtors raise the concern, acknowledged in the bill's own fair-treatment provisions, that some debtors could use the system to shed obligations they could partly pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households in genuine distress, the relief would be substantial: a faster, cheaper path out of unpayable debt, the ability to save a home or car, and freedom from private student loans. The real cost falls on lenders and, indirectly, on future borrowers through credit pricing. The bill tries to balance this with formulas that cap what debtors must pay and fair-treatment rules for creditors, but it was introduced without any hearing process, so its sweeping redesign was never tested or amended in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of a Congress that was about to end, sent to the Judiciary and Financial Services Committees, and neither committee took it up, so it expired without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2020 with Rep. David Cicilline on December 8, 2020 [S1].
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services Committee [S5].
Cicilline was the bill's only cosponsor [S4].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed; the action history shows no activity after the referrals, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders, mortgage holders, private student loan companies, and debt collectors keep the bankruptcy rules they operate under today, because the bill died without any committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer lenders, mortgage and student loan holders

for.name: Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 8, 2020, in the final weeks of the 116th Congress.

for.name: 1 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Rep. David Cicilline of Rhode Island).

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no vote ever occurred, so there is no record of how the parties would have split on it.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders and credit card issuers
industries.note: Under Chapter 10, unsecured claims like credit card debt would be dischargeable after a payment obligation capped by the debtor's income and assets, and debtors with no ability to pay could be discharged immediately. Lenders would recover less, which they would likely recoup through credit terms for everyone.

The bill allows modification of mortgages on all residences and lets debtors cure defaults in a residence plan without paying interest on arrearages, penalty rates, or late fees, while blocking foreclosure remedies unless the debtor falls 120 days behind. This undoes protections lenders have had since the 2005 bankruptcy law.

The bill would allow student loan debt to be discharged on equal terms with most other debt, ending the special treatment private student loans have enjoyed; the bill's findings argue this special treatment never lowered borrowers' financing costs.
Car loans could be reduced to the market value of the vehicle rather than the full loan balance, directly cutting what auto finance companies recover.

The bill targets what it calls illegal debt collection activity that undercuts the fresh start of bankruptcy, strengthens the discharge injunction, and voids pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers in confirmed plans.

The bill declares that a rent-to-own lessor has no interest in the covered property, letting debtors keep or return the goods as if they were unsecured, which removes the repossession leverage these stores rely on.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy trustees and consumer bankruptcy attorneys
industries.note: Titles IV and V fund the bankruptcy system and set trustee compensation, supporting the professionals who run cases; but streamlined no-plan cases and reduced paperwork would shrink billable work in routine filings.
